key_insight: Procedural skills can improve LLM agents overall, but their real impact must be decomposed into gains and regressions because added skills can also make agents worse.
engineering_relevance: For reliable office-automation agents, skill design should prioritize grounding and verification, since these matter more for avoiding failures than procedural instructions alone.
method: Compare agents with vs. without skills across ~6,000 runs.
Separate outcomes into regressions (solved without skills, failed with skills) and residual failures (failed in both cases).
Trace failure modes to identify osmosis, grounding displacement, and verification displacement.
evidence_signal: Across two office automation benchmarks and three harness stacks, the authors find regressions are large enough that the best skills often win mainly by causing fewer regressions, not more new successes.
watch_item: Results depend on careful artifact correction and trace analysis, so implementations should avoid assuming any skill is beneficial just because average success improves.
paper_title: The Regression Tax: Decomposing Why Skills Help and Hurt LLM Agents
